Vital Signs and the Device That Measures Each

Unit 2: Anatomy, Physiology, and Medical Terminology. Lesson 9 of 53 in BMET Academy.

A vital sign is one of the handful of numbers that say how a patient is doing right now. Clinicians read them constantly, and most of the equipment you will touch in your first year measures one of them. This lesson ties each number to its device and to the thing that most often makes it wrong.

The numbers and the boxes

Vital sign          Normal adult at rest      Measured by
Heart rate          60 to 100 beats/min       ECG monitor, pulse oximeter, NIBP module
Respiratory rate    12 to 20 breaths/min      monitor impedance channel, capnograph
Blood pressure      about 120/80 mmHg         NIBP cuff, or arterial line and transducer
SpO2                95 to 100%                pulse oximeter
Temperature         37 C (98.6 F)             electronic thermometer, monitor probe, infrared
EtCO2               35 to 45 mmHg             capnograph
Pain                0 to 10, patient reported  no device: the patient's own answer

Pain is on the list of things measured at the bedside and it is the one with no instrument. That is worth remembering, because a question that asks which vital sign has no sensor has exactly one answer.

Where the sensors go

  • ECG electrodes: on prepped skin over bone or firm tissue, not over a moving muscle, and in the arrangement the monitor expects for three or five leads.
  • NIBP cuff: upper arm, snug, with the bladder centered over the artery and the arm supported at heart level.
  • SpO2 probe: a finger, toe, or ear, with the two LEDs on one side and the photodiode that detects their light facing them through the tissue.
  • Temperature probe: the site the probe type is made for, oral, axillary, or rectal, with the right cover.
  • Capnography sampling line: in the breathing circuit for an intubated patient, or a nasal cannula for a patient breathing on their own.

The errors you will be called about

Most vital-sign calls are not broken equipment. They are physics meeting a real patient.

  • Wrong cuff size. A cuff too small for the arm reads high; too large reads low. The bladder should wrap about 80% of the arm.
  • Motion. A shivering or restless patient defeats both the oximeter and the cuff. The oximeter looks for a pulse-shaped change in light, and movement looks the same.
  • Cold fingers and poor circulation. No pulsing blood at the probe means no SpO2 reading, and the display says so with a weak or missing signal indicator. Nail polish and bright overhead light cause the same complaint.
  • Loose or dried-out electrodes. The classic false alarm: an electrode that has lifted shows a flat line or a lead-off message, and it gets reported as "the monitor says the patient has no heartbeat".
  • Mouth breathing on a nasal capnography cannula. The exhaled gas misses the sample port, so EtCO2 reads far too low on a patient who is breathing perfectly well.

The right first move for all of these is the same: look at the patient and the sensor before you suspect the box. If the patient looks fine and the sensor is wrong, the sensor is the fault.

Exam tip: when a reading is impossible but the patient is comfortable, suspect the interface, not the instrument: the electrode, the probe, the cuff, the line, or the site.
Remember
Heart rate 60 to 100, respiratory rate 12 to 20, blood pressure about 120/80 mmHg, SpO2 95 to 100%, temperature 37 C, EtCO2 35 to 45 mmHg, pain 0 to 10 with no device. Errors: wrong cuff size (small reads high), motion, cold fingers, loose electrodes, mouth breathing on a nasal capnography line. Check the patient and the sensor before the monitor.
Deeper explanation

Vital Signs and the Device That Measures Each, explained slowly

What a vital sign is for

A vital sign is a number that changes quickly when a patient gets worse. That is the whole reason this short list is measured again and again: it is an early warning system. Your job is to make sure the warning is true, because a monitor that cries wolf gets ignored, and an ignored monitor is a patient safety problem rather than an equipment problem.

The table to know cold

Vital sign          Normal adult at rest       Device                               Units
Heart rate          60 to 100                  ECG monitor, oximeter, NIBP module   beats per minute
Respiratory rate    12 to 20                   impedance channel, capnograph        breaths per minute
Blood pressure      about 120/80               NIBP cuff, arterial line             mmHg
SpO2                95 to 100                  pulse oximeter                       percent
Temperature         37 C (98.6 F)              thermometer, monitor probe, infrared C or F
EtCO2               35 to 45                   capnograph                           mmHg
Pain                0 to 10, as reported       none: the patient answers            a scale

Note the last row. Pain is recorded at the bedside and has no sensor, which makes it the answer to any question asking which vital sign no device measures.

Placement, and why each site is chosen

  • ECG electrodes go on clean, dry, prepped skin over bone or firm tissue. Over a moving muscle the electrode records the muscle, not the heart.
  • NIBP cuff goes on the upper arm with the bladder centered over the artery, the arm supported at heart level. A limb held above the heart reads low and a limb hanging below it reads high, which is why the position of the arm is part of the technique and not a detail.
  • SpO2 probe needs the light source and the detector facing each other through well-perfused tissue: a fingertip, a toe, an earlobe, or a foot on an infant.
  • Temperature probe must match its site and wear the right cover; an oral probe used rectally is a cross-contamination event, which is why the probes are color coded.
  • Capnography line goes in the circuit for an intubated patient or on a nasal cannula for a patient breathing on their own.

The five calls you will actually get

Complaint                        Usual cause                          First check
"blood pressure reads too high"  cuff too small for the arm           cuff size: the bladder wraps about 80% of the limb
"oximeter keeps dropping out"    motion, cold fingers, poor perfusion warm the site, move the probe, check the waveform
"monitor says no heartbeat"      an electrode lifted or dried out     look at the patient, then the electrodes
"EtCO2 is way too low"           mouth breathing on a nasal cannula   watch how the patient breathes
"temperature reads room temp"    probe off the patient                where the probe actually is

Every row has the same shape: the patient is fine and the interface is not. That is why the rule is to look at the patient first, the sensor second, the cable third, and the monitor last. It is also why swapping a probe or a lead set for a known-good one is the fastest diagnostic test in the building: one swap splits the problem in half.

What makes a verification, not just a guess

When you do check the monitor itself, use a patient simulator: it produces known ECG rates and amplitudes, an SpO2 value, a respiration rate, and a temperature, so you can compare the display against something traceable. NIBP accuracy needs a pressure standard, and EtCO2 needs a known calibration gas. Comparing one monitor against another monitor proves nothing, because you have no idea which one is wrong.
